summary: This informational RFC summarizes issues with the DNS A6 record, discusses its status, and moves RFC 2874 to Historic status. This gives clarity to implementers and operators.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS tried a fancy way to store IPv6 addresses that never caught on. This officially retires it.

questions: what happened to the a6 record
subtitle: Moving the A6 DNS record type to Historic status and explaining why.

tldr.problem: The IETF created two different ways to store IPv6 addresses in the DNS: AAAA records and A6 records. A6 had fundamental design problems: it caused slow lookups, was prone to failures, and created confusion in the DNS ecosystem.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6563 documents the known issues with A6, confirms it was rarely used in practice, and formally moves RFC 2874 (the A6 specification) from Experimental to Historic status.
tldr.outcome: This change clarifies that AAAA is the only standard way to represent IPv6 addresses in DNS. Implementers should not create new A6 support, and all existing A6 records should be removed.

facts.label: A6 query percentage
facts.value: Less than 1% of root server DNS queries

today: RFC 6563 was published in March 2012 and formally moved A6 to Historic status. AAAA is the Internet Standard for representing IPv6 addresses in the DNS and remains so today. The decision to deprecate A6 and standardize on AAAA was one of the key early decisions that helped simplify IPv6 deployment and is now universally accepted across the internet industry.

sections.title: Two Paths to IPv6 in DNS
sections.content:
When IPv6 came to the internet, the DNS needed a way to store IPv6 addresses. The IETF created two approaches: AAAA records (a straightforward 128-bit IPv6 address field) specified in 1995, and A6 records (a complex scheme allowing components to be stored separately and referenced across domain boundaries) specified in 2000.

A6 was designed to support renumbering and multihoming—the ability to change network prefixes and have multiple network connections without updating every DNS record. However, having two different record types led to confusion about which to implement and deploy, potentially delaying IPv6 adoption. In 2002, A6 was moved to Experimental status by RFC 3363 to signal that AAAA was the preferred approach.
sections.plainLanguage: The internet had two ways to write down IPv6 addresses: a simple one and a fancy one. The fancy one seemed like it would help with network changes, but it was complicated and nobody used it.

sections.title: Why A6 Didn't Work
sections.content:
Resolution latency: A6 records form chains where each link points to another location in the DNS. Resolving a chain means making multiple separate queries, each adding delay. In the worst case, a long chain could take many seconds to resolve, frustrating users.

Resolution failure: Each query in a chain can fail independently. With an N-link chain, the overall probability of failure is the sum of all individual failure probabilities. Additionally, if any link fails, determining where the failure occurred takes unpredictable time.

Cross-administrative complexity: A6 chains often pointed across zone and organizational boundaries. Experience with other pointer types (glue records, PTR records) showed that out-of-zone pointers are rarely maintained properly by other organizations.

Maintenance burden: Changes to shared components of an A6 record affect multiple IPv6 addresses, creating complicated dependency relationships. Multiple subcomponents may have different time-to-live (TTL) values, complicating cache management.

Confusion: If both AAAA and A6 were deployed, DNS clients would not know which to query. Running both in parallel could return conflicting results.

Security risks: Attacking a single subcomponent of an A6 chain could affect many hosts. A6 chains could also create infinite loops if pointers referenced each other circularly.
sections.plainLanguage: A6 chains were slow because they required many lookups. They broke easily, were hard to maintain, and could loop forever. If you used both AAAA and A6, you never knew which answer to believe.

sections.title: Current State and Transition
sections.content:
A6 was never widely deployed. Statistics from root DNS servers show less than 1% of all queries request A6 records (roughly 60% request A records for IPv4, 20-25% request AAAA for IPv6). The small amount of A6 traffic likely comes from older BIND9 versions (9.0–9.2) that were configured by default to make A6 queries, and from legacy Linux/glibc implementations that have not been updated in over a decade.

RFC 6563 moves RFC 2874 from Experimental to Historic status, clearly signaling that A6 must not be implemented or deployed. Implementers should:

  • Remove A6 handling from all new or updated DNS implementations
  • Delete all existing A6 records from DNS
  • Treat A6 queries as unknown record type queries (the same response as for any unrecognized DNS record type)

Since there are no known production uses of A6-only clients, this transition poses negligible risk. DNS will be simpler, faster, and more secure without A6.
sections.plainLanguage: Hardly anyone used A6 in practice. The new rule is: delete the A6 records you have, do not build A6 into new programs, and ignore A6 queries if you get them.

sections.title: Outcome: AAAA as the Standard
sections.content:
By moving A6 to Historic, the IETF provided clarity to DNS implementers and operators. AAAA records are the sole standard for representing IPv6 addresses in the DNS. This decision resolved a decade of ambiguity and simplified the DNS ecosystem.

The move eliminated future investment in a failed technology and reduced confusion for system administrators, software vendors, and internet users. AAAA support is now universal in DNS software and services.
sections.plainLanguage: Now everyone agrees: use AAAA for IPv6 addresses in DNS, and forget about A6. This makes the internet simpler.
